project.name: Not Arbitrary 13 — Worn Down, or Cut in Pieces

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Japanese writes its syllables in two sets of letters, and both sets are Chinese characters in disguise. One set was written too fast. The other was cut into pieces.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, a little conspiratorial. A small pause before 'One set was written too fast', and give the last two sentences the same shape.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Japan first wrote with borrowed Chinese characters, and for its own words it often used them only for their sounds, the way you might write 'I can see' with a picture of an eye, a tin can and the sea.
entries.direction: Plain and clear through the first half. Light and a little playful on the eye, the tin can and the sea.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: It worked, but it took a lot of ink. One eighth-century book of poems uses almost twenty different characters for the very same syllable.
entries.direction: Dry. A small stress on 'almost twenty' and on 'the very same'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Buddhist monks, adding reading notes to Chinese scriptures, needed a shorthand. So they kept one small piece of each character and dropped the rest.
entries.direction: A new thread, so lift slightly. Matter of fact on 'and dropped the rest'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: From a character that means 'add', they kept the left-hand side. That piece became a letter of its own, and it has hardly changed since.
entries.direction: Simple and warm. Say the word 'add' as the ordinary English word, clearly.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: From a character meaning 'roof', they kept the roof itself, the little shelter drawn across the top.
entries.direction: Gentle, a little pleased with the detail.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: And from the character for 'profit', which is grain standing beside a knife, they kept the knife. So two of these letters are still pictures: a roof, and a knife.
entries.direction: Build slightly across the first sentence. A small beat after 'still pictures', then land 'a roof, and a knife' simply.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Meanwhile, at court, people wrote the same characters whole, but with a brush and at speed. Written that fast, a character stops being separate strokes and becomes one flowing gesture.
entries.direction: The turn of the film. Slow down. A definite pause after 'Meanwhile, at court'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The character for 'add' kept its left side almost as it was, while its little box shrank to a flick of the brush.
entries.direction: Unhurried, a small smile on 'a flick of the brush'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The roof shrank to a single dot, and everything underneath it ran together into one curve.
entries.direction: Flowing, as if tracing the curve. Land 'one curve' lightly.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The grain and the knife each wore down to a single stroke, standing side by side.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: That flowing set became the writing of the women at court, and a thousand years ago one of them used it to write The Tale of Genji, often called the first novel.
entries.direction: Warm and a little wondering. Genji is GEN-jee, with a hard G.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Three characters, and two letters from each: one worn down by a hurrying brush, one cut to a single piece by a monk short of room.
entries.direction: Gather it up. Warm, not a summary read.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Every Japanese sentence still mixes all three: characters whole, worn down, and cut.
entries.direction: Land it and stop. No lift at the end.
